https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.title: Lord Alli attends Labour conference despite donations row
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.text:
Thank you for joining our coverage of the first full day of Labour’s annual party conference.
I will be back early tomorrow to bring you all the latest from Liverpool.
Angela Rayner has said taxpayers “can’t keep funding” social housing under the current Right to Buy discounts, writes Ruby Hinchcliffe.
The deputy prime minister, who benefitted from the Right to Buy scheme herself, said there was “no point in me having the biggest wave in a generation of council homes through one way, only not to be able to replace them when they go out the door the next”.
Ms Rayner, who is also the Government’s housing secretary, has set a 1.5m house building target for the next five years – much of which she hopes will be made up of new, affordable social homes.
At a fringe event in Labour’s Party Conference, Ms Rayner added: “We’ve got to have a fair system. Now I think if you’ve raised your kids and lived in the house for decades, and you want to buy the house, I think it’s absolutely reasonable and right that people should be given that opportunity.
“But I also believe we can’t have a situation where taxpayers are funding social housing and we can’t replace it because of the discount. I’m starting a conversation on that, to make sure we can fix it so we can make sure we keep our social housing into the future.”
In 2007, Ms Rayner used the Right to Buy scheme to buy her former council house in Stockport, Greater Manchester, for £79,000 after claiming a 25pc discount. She then sold the property eight years later, in 2015, for £48,500 more than she paid for it.
The Housing Secretary has committed to a consultation on Right to Buy, set to launch on the day of the October Budget.
Thank you for joining our coverage of the first full day of Labour’s annual party conference.
I will be back early tomorrow to guide you through all the latest from Liverpool.
A speech by Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor, will be the main focus on the second full day of Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool tomorrow.
Ms Reeves is likely to defend her tough approach towards the public finances, having stripped 10 million retirees of the winter fuel allowance.
The Conservatives have set up a parody GoFundMe page called ‘GoFundKeir’ in the wake of a row over his donations.
The campaign website highlights donations to the Prime Minister including £4,000 in tickets to a Taylor Swift concert and £2,485 in new glasses.
“As you can see, Keir leads a modest lifestyle which needs to be properly funded,” the website says.
“Donate to poor old Keir.”
The head of the Muslim Council of Britain has suggested Lord Alli is being demonised because he is a Muslim, writes Jacob Freedland.
Asked if the scrutiny over the Labour peer and donor was because of his faith, Zara Mohammed, the organisation’s general secretary, told The Telegraph: “What we’re seeing from some media outlets and commentators is the demonisation of anyone in public space who is Muslim.
“I can’t comment on the clothes issue itself, but there definitely does seem to be this narrative that the role of Muslims in public life is always sinister, is always devious and always got some ulterior motive.
“We know there’s lots of lobbyist backers, lots of scandals in our politics that need to be dealt with and politicians should be held to account, but it does always feel like if there is a Muslim lobby group then it’s always doing something sinister.”
Liz Kendall has said she wants to see a “fair deal” for social care workers “in my heart and in my bones”, writes our Political Correspondent Amy Gibbons.
The Work and Pensions Secretary told an event on the fringes of the Labour conference: “This is a huge issue of equality. It is a huge issue for social justice, and it is a huge issue for women. And as a proud feminist, I know that care has always been undervalued because it’s what women do. And we say no more, no more.”
She said the UK will never get its economy growing if “people can’t work because they have to look after their loved ones”.
“I’ll never stop fighting for you, I’ll never stop campaigning for you, and together we’ll make that change happen,” she added.
Wes Streeting has urged people to “give us a bit of time” when it comes to fixing social care.
The Health Secretary said Labour is thinking “really carefully” about what can be done both during this Parliament and over the course of the next decade.
He told a fringe event at the party’s annual conference: “If there’s one kind of point of humility I think we’ve all got to reflect on in the Labour Party, it’s that the Labour Party, the Conservative Party, the Liberal Democrats, the SNP, we’ve all been in Government in different parts of the UK over the last 20 years or so.
“And none of us have actually properly gripped this and delivered the long-term change, the long-term solutions for social care that the country is desperately crying out for.
“I know people are hungry for change... I just say two things. Firstly, we’ve only been here for two months. Give us a bit of time. But secondly, you should take from the last couple of months that there is a quiet determination at the centre of our team in the Department of Health and Social Care and more broadly with the Government to make sure that we get this right.”
The leading Labour rebel over the winter fuel allowance has said that she is “sickened” by the revelations surrounding donations which she said “grates against the values of the Labour Party”, writes Genevieve Holl-Allen.
Rachael Maskell, MP for York Central, said that the Labour Party was “created to fight for the needs of others, not self” as she contrasted the scrapping of the universal winter fuel payment with the accepting of freebies.
Writing on X, Ms Maskell said: “I have been sickened by revelations of ‘donations’. It grates against the values of the Labour Party, created to fight for the needs of others, not self.
“Meanwhile pensioners are having their Winter Fuel Payments taken, risking going cold. I trust conference votes to change this.”
Britain’s pension industry is facing a stampede of savers attempting to withdraw lump sums from their retirement pots amid rising fears of Rachel Reeves’ potential tax raid.
Standard Life, AJ Bell and Royal London are understood to be among the pension giants already receiving a surge in inquiries about tax-free withdrawals ahead of next month’s Budget.
Sir Steve Webb, a former pensions minister, said there is “widespread concern” among the public about the Chancellor possibly reducing the amount of tax-free cash that pension savers can withdraw.
Adam Mawardi and Tim Wallace have more here
Lord Alli is attending Labour’s annual party conference in Liverpool despite a row about his donations to Sir Keir Starmer and his top team.
The Labour peer, who is Sir Keir’s biggest personal donor, has given tens of thousands of pounds in clothing to the Prime Minister and Victory, his wife.
Sir Keir broke parliamentary rules by initially failing to declare thousands of pounds in clothes for Lady Starmer from the peer.
A source confirmed to The Telegraph that Lord Alli is in Liverpool after he was spotted at an event on Saturday night.
There is no suggestion Lord Alli has done anything wrong and he has been contacted by The Telegraph for comment.
Sue Gray is to miss the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, writes our Political Editor Ben Riley-Smith.
Sir Keir Starmer’s influential chief of staff has found herself at the centre of a saga about her pay and Downing Street in-fighting.
Earlier this week, it was revealed that Ms Gray is being paid more than the Prime Minister, with a salary of £170,000 compared with Sir Keir’s £167,000.
A Downing Street source confirmed to The Telegraph that Ms Gray would not be attending the Labour conference, which runs from today until Wednesday.
You can read the full story here
Liz Kendall has insisted that the issue of child poverty is a “personal priority”, as she was met with demands by campaigners to abolish the two-child benefit cap, writes Genevieve Holl-Allen.
The Government’s refusal to abolish the benefit limit sparked the first rebellion of Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership, and seven MPs who voted against the Government on the issue were suspended from Labour.
The chief executive of the Child Poverty Action Group (CPAG) told the Work and Pensions’ Secretary to remove the two-child cap, adding: “Every day it stays in place, another 109 children are dragged into poverty.”
Alison Garnham told a fringe event: “None of us want to hear stories about how complex child poverty is and how we need to look at the root causes.
“Come on. It’s about money. I think we all know,” she added.
Ms Kendall told the event that the Government had set up the child poverty task force to tackle the issue, adding: “Let me tell you loud and clear, this is a priority for this new Labour government, and it is. It is a personal priority for me.”
A black Labour MP has said the government were wrong to hesitate over describing the summer riots as Islamophobic, writes Jacob Freedland.
Speaking on an anti-racism panel at a Labour fringe event, Dawn Butler said: “We have to progress. We should’ve called it Islamophobia from the very beginning. We shouldn’t hesitate about that.”
The MP for Brent East also said that her mum was “triggered” by the riots, recalling one instance when she was on her way to visit and her mother said: “No don’t come”.
Ms Butler said she thought: “Oh my gosh. She’s completely triggered.”
Liz Kendall has said she is “more worried” about children’s mental health now than she was immediately after the Covid pandemic.
The Work and Pensions Secretary said the Government would look “much more deeply” at solving the youth mental health crisis as part of tackling child poverty.
Speaking at an event by the Child Poverty Action Group, the MP for Leicester West said: “But (with) mental health, I am more worried now than I was immediately after Covid.
“And don’t forget, Leicester was locked down the longest in Covid, about the mental health consequences for children and young people, that’s something we need to look much more deeply at.”
A Left-wing former member of Labour’s ruling executive body had a swipe at Lord Alli as he accused Sir Keir Starmer of learning from “Mussolini’s grandchildren” on how to deal with immigration, writes Jacob Freedland.
Mish Rahman, who sat on the National Executive Committee between 2020 and 2024, opened his speech at an anti-racism panel at a Labour fringe event in Liverpool by joking: “It’s good to be at a fringe where people are not wearing designer clothes donated by Waheed Alli.”
The activist went on to castigate the party’s leadership for failing to enact left-wing policies, stating: “What is the moral purpose of our nation? It’s not to keep children in poverty; it’s not to freeze pensioners; it’s not to dress up in thousands and thousands of pounds worth of gear and shiny suits donated by Waheed [Alli]; it’s not to learn from the grandchildren of Mussolini on how to deal with immigration. That is not the moral purpose of our nation.”
Israel could face further sanctions over settler violence in the West Bank, David Lammy suggested in his speech.
The Foreign Secretary told a fringe event at Labour’s conference in Liverpool he was “deeply” concerned by “escalatory behaviour” in the region.
“I’m deeply, deeply worried by the growing violence and settler violence that we see in the West Bank,” Mr Lammy said.
”I’m in discussions with G7 partners, particular European partners on that. I’m not announcing further sanctions today, but that is kept under close review.”
A Left-wing Labour MP has suggested Labour risks feeding anti-immigration sentiment by going along with the “Right-wing analysis” of the issue, writes Jacob Freedland.
Speaking at an anti-racism panel fringe event at Labour conference in Liverpool, Richard Burgon said: “When you ask voters what issue is most important to them, a lot of the time people say it’s immigration.
“There was a period when this didn’t happen and that was between 2015-2019 [when Jeremy Corbyn was leader of the party]. Why was that? We didn’t go along with the Right-wing analysis of immigration.
“If people see on TV the politicians from the party they support saying immigration is a problem, it’s no wonder that when you knock on their doors they say immigration is a problem.
“We’ve got to be careful not to feed that cycle. They need an analysis that says [our problems] are not because of migrants.”
David Lammy concluded: “Conference, the world we face is filled with disorder, conflicts in Europe, Africa and the Middle East, great power competition, an increasingly assertive China and a climate emergency.
“But together, we have a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to make the change we want to see not just in Britain but in Europe and in the world.
“Just as Clem Attlee’s 1945 government rebuild the country after the Second World War, just as Harold Wilson’s government in the 1960s seized the white heat of technology in the face of the future, and just as Tony Blair and Gordon Brown’s government transformed our public services, we in Keir Starmer’s public services have the opportunity to make history with a decade of national renewal... A Britain reconnected, a Britain back where it belongs.”
David Lammy turned to the Israel-Hamas conflict, calling the Oct 7 attacks “horrific” as he called out “Hamas terrorists”.
“What has followed those atrocities is horrific war. Tens of thousands of Palestinian women and children killed and injured. Their homes turned to rubble, leaving Gaza a vision of hell on earth. Meanwhile dozens of Israelis remain cruelly held captive, and Israel faces threats from all angles with Iran and its proxies seeking to wipe Israel off the map.
“Conference, I know like me you are desperate to see the conflict in the Middle East come to an end. And this Labour Government has already made clear Britain’s principles.”
He noted “no previous foreign secretary had even used” the words “immediate ceasefire”, saying: “We have used the full weight of Britain’s diplomacy, to push to protect civilians now, get all the hostages out now, and get unrestricted aid into Gaza now...
“We have never lost sight of the end goal - an irreversible pathway towards a two-state solution.”
David Lammy, the Foreign Secretary, told delegates: “If the West does not demonstrate it can outlast Putin, it does not only threaten Ukraine’s democracy, it threatens us all.
“We need to show Putin that Britain and its allies are not going anywhere which is why this Government has increased support to Ukraine, and we’ve committed £3bn a year in military aid as long as it takes.
“And it’s why I told Zelensky, this Labour Government will always stand with his courageous hope.”
Mr Lammy added: “We need to send another message to Vladimir Putin. Your interference in our democracy, promoting disinformation and encouraging disorder on our streets, encouraging kleptocrats to store their ill-gotten gains in our property market, must end.”
David Lammy told Labour’s conference: “When the Labour Government hosted 45 European leaders at Blenheim Palace to reset our relationship with Europe, we said Britain is back. When we restored the funding to UNRWA for their work in Gaza, what did we say, conference? Britain is back.
“And when we stood up for international law when it was not easy, what did we say? Britain is back. In my first four months I’ve visited 10 countries, engaged 20 world leaders and over 40 foreign ministers. And what did I tell them? Britain is back.”
Mr Lammy said: “We will seek a new, broad ambitious UK-EU security pact on shared threats that we face, enshrining a new geopolitical partnership because Britain is back. A leading nation in Europe once again.”
David Lammy told Labour conference: “My job is to tell a new story about the United Kingdom, a story of openness, a story of the future, a story of hope that will reconnect Britain with the world once more...”
“The Conservative Party misused the British state, handing out crony contracts to their mates, crashing the economy with their delusional ideology. For 14 years the Conservative Party damaged our reputation abroad, threatening to break international law, threatening our European friends and treating them as our foes.
“For 14 long years the Conservative Party abandoned our values, tearing up climate commitments, threatening to leave the European Convention on Human Rights. On my first weekend as Foreign Secretary, when I travelled to Germany, to Poland, to Sweden, in less than 48 hours, I was proud to say Britain is back.”
David Lammy, the Foreign Secretary, said everyone at Labour conference had their own story, and he grew up “in the shadow of Tottenham’s Broadwater Estate”.
“Life was not always easy, my mum struggling to put food on our table, skinheads shouting abuse as we walked by, my father leaving when I was 12.
“He didn’t leave me very much but he did leave me a map, and that was an atlas which I put on my bedroom wall. And from this wall I learned about the countries my ancestors had come from, transported from west Africa to Guyana as part of the transatlantic slave trade, long before my parents moved from Guyana to Britain to help rebuild Britain after the Second World War.
“Conference, I can’t tell you how it feels to stand here today, a black working-class man from Tottenham, a child of the great Windrush generation, now back on this stage as the Foreign Secretary in a Labour Government.”
Angela Rayner has urged people not to forget scandals and division under the last Conservative government amid Labour’s own controversies over donations.
The Deputy Prime Minister denied she broke any rules over the donated use of a New York apartment owned by the Labour peer Lord Alli, who has also donated thousands of pounds in clothes to Sir Keir Starmer.
In her keynote speech on the first day of Labour’s annual party conference in Liverpool, Ms Rayner vowed her party would show “no complacency”.
“We won because we had the courage to change our party, the discipline to make hard decisions, and the determination to remain united,” she said.
“And now, change begins. Even now, especially now, there will be no complacency. Don’t forget where they did - partygate, Covid contracts, lies, division, scapegoating and the unfunded tax cuts for the rich that crashed our economy. Don’t forget any of it.
“The Tories failed Britain and tried to cover it up. A crater in the heart of Britain’s economy, a puncture in the pocket of every working family and a £22 billion black hole, and not as much an apology, let alone an acceptance, from the Tories.”
Bridget Phillipson has admitted that Taylor Swift concert tickets were a “hard one to turn down” because one of her children was “keen” to go, writes Genevieve Holl-Allen.
Ms Phillipson accepted two tickets and hospitality worth £522 to the Eras Tour from the Football Association in August, and declared the gift in the register of interests.
The Education Secretary said that given the enthusiasm of her children and the “big demand” for tickets to the sold-out concert, “it’s hard to say no”.
She told ITV: “Look, I’ll be honest it was a hard one to turn down. I appreciate there was big demand for the tickets, it was a privilege to be there.
“One of my children was keen to go along. It’s hard to say no when you’re offered tickets to something in those circumstances, but it was declared, I’ve been clear about that. But I do recognise that I’m in a fortunate position to be able to receive that.”
The Ukrainian Ambassador has said Ukraine should be able to hit military targets in Russia out of “self-defence”.
Valerii Zaluzhnyi told Labour’s conference in Liverpool: “As an ex-commander in chief, I know firsthand that we desperately need the capabilities for our people to prevail in this war.
“If Russia fires missiles at any targets in Ukraine, be it civilian or military, then it is Ukraine’s absolute right to respond in kind by hitting military targets within Russia.
“This is what Article 51 of the United Nations charter is about. This is not escalation, it is about the principle of self-defence, building on what we might call Bevan’s ten principles.”
The Ukrainian Ambassador to the UK is currently making a surprise appearance at the Labour conference in Liverpool.
Valerii Zaluzhnyi said: “I want to take this opportunity to thank the Prime Minister, the Foreign Secretary and the Defence Secretary for their commitment to the Ukrainian people.
“The Labour Party has a long history of opposing fascism and terrorism.”
He said Labour ensured Britain remained “resolute” in the 1940s, adding: “It was Bevin who understood the importance of strength... Bevin’s legacy includes the founding of Nato, the cornerstone of European security.
“He would have understood the urgent need for Ukraine’s fast-track membership of Nato as a necessity that should be recognised.”
Anneliese Dodds has said Labour is “really serious” about introducing a conversion therapy ban that is “clear about its scope”, writes Amy Gibbons.
The equalities minister told a fringe event at the Labour conference that enabling people to discuss their gender identity or sexuality with a therapist or a teacher is a “good thing”.
But she said “when we see a practice that is seeking to force someone to change, that is when it becomes, obviously, a conversion practice”.
She added: “It’s not about exploration. It’s something very different. So we’re working hard on this. You hopefully will have seen it mentioned in the King’s Speech.
“It’s something that we’re really serious about because it is abuse, we’re determined to act against it, and we think that, frankly, the people who have been subject to it have had so many promises on this... they don’t need promises anymore, they need to see action.”
Darren Jones, the Chief Secretary to the Treasury, said there was “power at work through collectivism”.
He recalled his grandparents growing up in a council flat, and his family having worked on the docks in Bristol.
Mr Jones said Sir Tony Blair’s “education, education, education” mantra had to be a priority for the new Government.
Attendees at Labour’s conference here in Liverpool are able to pick themselves up an Ed Miliband-themed cappucino at the Renewable UK stall in the exhibition, which uses green printing technology.
Our Political Reporter Genevieve Holl-Allen was among the first to try one out.
It took quite some soul-searching for Nick Bowyer to cast his first ever vote for Labour, writes Rosa Silverman, as Hitchin went red for the first time.
The honeymoon period Sir Keir Starmer might have hoped for, however, has proved to be remarkably short.
Following a series of controversial moves – scrapping the winter fuel payment for all but the poorest pensioners chief among them – goodwill towards the new Government seems to be already ebbing away.
This month, an Ipsos poll found support for Labour had slipped four points to 36 per cent, while almost half (46 per cent) of people viewed Prime Minister Starmer unfavourably - his joint worst rating since he became party leader.
Rosa Silverman has more here
Pat McFadden, the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, told delegates Labour must “never go back” to the party it was under Jeremy Corbyn.
“It is change worth having and change worth fighting for. Now, it won’t always be easy, and it won’t always be quick.
“But if we hold true to the lessons of our victory this year. If we vow never to go back, not back to the kind of party the Tories enjoyed beating.
“Then we won’t go back to the kind of Tory Government that we had for so many years which left us with the legacy they did.
“People will judge us at the next election on whether their family is better off, whether their public services are working better, whether we are rebuilding the country. The same things uponwhich we should judge ourselves.”
The Defence Secretary will announce an end to “outdated and unnecessary” Army entry requirements in his conference speech tomorrow.
Plans will be put forward to dramatically speed up offers to applicants as Labour said more than 100 recruitment criteria had been scrapped since the party won the general election in July.
These include red tape that had blocked some hay fever, eczema and acne sufferers from serving their country.
Mr Healey said: “Our Armed Forces rightly set the highest standards and with Labour that will continue. At the same time, we will unblock the bottlenecks, the needless red tape and delays which are turning great talent away from our forces.
“As the world changes, and threats evolve, we also need to ensure our recruitment is right for the 21st century. That’s why we will remove unnecessary barriers and fast-track bright candidates into cyber defence to help face down Putin’s online aggression.
“Alongside the largest pay rise in 20 years for existing troops, Labour is getting on with fixing the foundations of our armed forces and supporting the brave men and women who keep Britain safe.”
A new Labour MP who has worked as a GP for 30 years has said he will vote to legalise assisted dying when the choice is put to the Commons, writes Amy Gibbons.
Speaking at a fringe event at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, Dr Simon Opher said he saw the practice as “just another tool in palliative care”.
The legalisation of assisted dying was brought a step closer this month after another MP won a ballot to introduce a Private Member’s Bill aimed at reforming Britain’s “archaic laws”.
Asked how he would vote on the policy, Dr Opher said: “I am actually a supporter of assisted dying, I would vote for it. The only reason for that is I think it’s just another tool in palliative care. A lot of patients I’ve talked to have said that they’d like to be able to do it, but they probably wouldn’t use it.
“And I think the statistics from Australia particularly is that it gives a patient some sort of reassurance that if they get to that stage, when it’s too much, there is a way that they can do it. There’s lots of different arguments there. But most people who have gone through that process in Australia do not take their own lives because of palliative care there, but it’s very reassuring for them. So that’s why I support it.”
Hollie Ridley, Labour’s new general secretary, said it was “an honour to be on stage in front of the very people who delivered one of the biggest general election victories in British history”.
“I was so proud to stand alongside you as we sent over 400 Labour MPs to Westminster and put Keir Starmer into Number 10,” she told the main conference hall.
“And I am proud to stand before you now as only the third woman to be nominated as the party’s general secretary.
“Let me be clear, the work to win a second term starts right now... The 2024 playbook is done. It cannot be used again.”
This from Esther McVey, a former common sense minister:
Allies must show “guts” and “nerve” in their support for Ukraine, David Lammy has said after the country’s ambassador to Britain warned permission to use western missiles within Russia was “critical” for Kyiv’s success.
Speaking at a Labour Party fringe event alongside Ukraine’s ambassador to the UK, Valerii Zaluzhnyi, he warned it was a “critical time” for allies to show “fortitude” and “patience” in bolstering Ukraine’s defence.
“This is a critical time for nerve and for guts and for patience and for fortitude on behalf of allies who stand with Ukraine,” Mr Lammy said.
“I am not going to, as Foreign Secretary, of course, comment on operational detail, because that can only aid Putin.
“But there is a very real-time discussion across allies about how we can support Ukraine as we head into the winter.”
The UK and US have stopped short of explicitly giving Kyiv permission to fire western long-range missiles - such as Britain’s Storm Shadow weapons - at targets within Russia despite repeated pleas from the country’s government.
Rhetoric from Labour politicians “fuelled” attacks on refugees and migrants during the summer riots, a union general secretary claimed, Genevieve Holl-Allen writes.
Matt Wrack, the general secretary of the Fire Brigade Union, said that behind the riots “lay some very nasty racism and nasty Islamophobia” which he blamed on “mainstream politics”, including from Labour.
Speaking at a fringe event hosted by the Morning Star, a socialist newspaper, Mr Wrack said: “I think we have to be very clear that those behind those riots lay some very nasty racism and nasty Islamophobia and attacks on migrants and attacks on refugees that have been fuelled by people in mainstream politics and sadly, unfortunately, occasionally by Labour politicians in mainstream politics as well.
“And we need to call that out and challenge it. But the other side of those riots is again a deeply worrying concern to our movement, because those riots also fed off a lack of hope and a lack of future in many communities in de-industrialised parts of the country where there are no decent jobs, or prospects of decent jobs, where there are no decent homes, or prospects of these homes where public services are falling apart and have done because of the decimation of the past 14 years.”
The union chief warned: “If a Labour government comes in and does nothing to address those concerns, then they will feed the fuels of division and hatred that led to those outbursts of the riot.”
Angela Rayner concluded her speech by saying: “On July 4, people entrusted us the task of change and hope won. Now is our moment, not just to say, to do.
“Labour governments of the past took on this same challenge at a time when Britain desperately needed change.
“They deserved a better Britain when the odds were stacked against them and that is exactly what this Labour government must deliver once again. So conference, let’s get on with it.”
Angela Rayner told attendees: “Today, I’m proud to announce the next step in our devolution revolution.
“This Government will change the future of the north of England so northerners will no longer be dictated to from Whitehall.
“We will be the Government to complete devolution in the north, change will be irreversible, and I will get it done. And as a proud northerner, this milestone is personal to me.”
A union chief has said Sir Keir Starmer’s handling of the two child benefit cap and winter fuel payments have exposed his “ineptitude” at governing, reports Genevieve Holl-Allen.
Matt Wrack, the general secretary of the Fire Brigade Union, accused the Government of a “ridiculous approach” to the issue of poverty and suggested that “smart Alecs” advising the government on the winter fuel allowance should be fired.
Speaking at a fringe event, Mr Wrack said: “I think the treatment of the question of poverty has been not just appalling from the point of view of any sort of socialist perspective, but also politically inept as well.
“I think the approach to the two child limit, the winter fuel payments, has exposed the incoming Government to millions of people as being out of touch with the priorities that ordinary voters have.
“And it baffled people, talking to journalists who are baffled by how Labour has handled this. Well, that raises the other question of ineptitude, because actually, it didn’t need to have been done, and it’s almost being done to show how tough they are.”
He added: “You can predict it now that over the winter people will die, and there will be front page stories about an elderly person, and the headline will be something like ‘killed by Starmer cruelty’... And if the smart Alecs who give advice to the Labour leadership haven’t woken up to that, then frankly they shouldn’t be in their positions.”
This summer’s riots show the “mountain” the Government has to claim, Angela Rayner said in her Labour conference speech.
“I’m under no illusion about the mountain we have to climb,” Ms Rayner said.
“We all saw that this summer, violent extremists preyed on our communities and local councils were picking up the pieces. Local leadership is the foundation of strong communities. And that’s why I put local government back where it belongs, at the heart of my department’s name and missions.”
She added: “Keir and I are determined to end this Whitehall-knows-best approach and trust those with skin in the game... We will seize this moment and finally complete that irreversible shift in opportunity, power and wealth across the whole country.
“It’s why we can deliver, how we can deliver, real sustained change for every region, and Labour mayors are already proving it.”
Angela Rayner said the Grenfell Tower fire in which 72 people died was a “fateful failure of market and state, and a tragedy that was never happened again”.
“It’s unacceptable that we have thousands of buildings still wrapped in unsafe cladding seven years after Grenfell.
“And that is why we will bring forward a new remediation action plan this afternoon to speed up the process, and we’ll pursue those responsible without fear or favour.”
Turning to the Tories’ record on housing, Angela Rayner said: “14 years of Tory chaos has not just left its mark on people’s jobs but on homes too.
“Not enough are being built. The Tories failed to meet their targets year after year after year... Leaseholders left at the mercy of eye-watering charges, renters stay in damp and moldy homes, and homelessness is all around us.
“The simple aspiration for safe, secure and affordable homes, is further out of reach than ever. And we can’t go on like this. So change must begin at home.
“We’re tackling the Tories’ housing emergency, we will get Britain building and we’ll build decent homes for working people. Our long-term plan will free leaseholders from the tyranny of a medieval system, and a cross-government task force will end homelessness.”
Angela Rayner made a joke about Sir Keir Starmer’s toolmaker father, which became one of the Prime Minister’s key motifs during his election campaign.
“Now you may have heard me mention I was a trade unionist and if you didn’t know that, I should probably tell you that Keir’s dad was a toolmaker,” Ms Rayner said.
“And if you didn’t know his dad was a toolmaker, I probably need to tell you that he’s Prime Minister.
Angela Rayner rattles off a list of Labour’s changes in government so far.
“80 days in government, and we’ve been busy,” she said.
“A devolution revolution, a bill to deliver new rights and protections for renters. Planning reform to get Britain building, a landmark review to fix our NHS, a child poverty Task Force, 100 new specialist officers to tackle criminals, an end to one word Ofsted inspections.
“Ending the ban on onshore wind and fines for bosses polluting our waters, bills to kickstart Great British Energy, and to prevent another Liz Truss disastrous mini-Budget, to put buses in local hands and bring rail into public ownership. Conference, change has begun.”
Angela Rayner told delegates: “We won because we had the courage to change our party, the discipline to make hard decisions, and the determination to remain united And now, change begins.
“Even now, especially now, there will be no complacency. Don’t forget where they did - partygate, Covid contracts, lies, division, scapegoating and the unfunded tax cuts for the rich that crashed our economy. Don’t forget any of it.
“The Tories failed Britain and tried to cover it up. A crater in the heart of Britain’s economy, a puncture in the pocket of every working family and a £22 billion black hole, and not as much an apology, let alone an acceptance, from the Tories.”
Joking about Kemi Badenoch’s war of words with David Tennant, she said: “After three months as shadow housing secretary, she’s finally expressed the concern about a tenant. It’s just a pity it’s David Tennant.”
She claimed Ms Badenoch was “doing deals with the Daleks” after her public spat with the Doctor Who actor.
A visibly moved Angela Rayner thanked a former trade union colleague who introduced and said “I’ll try not to get too emotional”.
“12 months ago, I stood there and said, I hope that never again open conference as the Deputy Leader of the Opposition do. So, it’s an absolute great honor to stand here today as your deputy prime minister.
“And it’s an honour to open the first conference of a Labour government. And I want to start off with my first thanks which are to the British people. You entrusted us with the task of change and we will not forget it.
“You kept faith with us, and we kept faith with you. And let me thank all of you in this room, and my brilliant ministerial team who are already delivering on their promises.”
Ms Rayner added: “They thought our party was history, but this year, conference, we made history together.”
A video plays shortly before Angela Rayner’s speech showing a montage of the Deputy Prime Minister out and about during the general election campaign.
Set to electronic music, the clip included shots of Ms Rayner meeting Gordon Brown, the former Labour prime minister, and getting the vote out alongside Sir Keir Starmer.
The slogan of this year’s Labour conference in Liverpool is “change begins”.
It is Sir Keir Starmer’s way of trying to show his Government is already making progress on his priorities after Labour ran on the one-word general election slogan of “change” almost three months ago.
Having defended the party - and her own use of a donated New York apartment - on this morning’s broadcast round, Angela Rayner, the Deputy Prime Minister, will address Labour conference in a few minutes’ time.
You can follow all the action at the top of this live blog.
A former Just Stop Oil backer has said Labour is “meeting my hopes” on carrying out a green agenda, writes Jacob Freedland.
Dale Vince, an eco-industrialist who ceased funding Just Stop Oil, the green pressure group, in Oct 2023 to become a Labour donor, told the Telegraph: “They’re meeting my hopes. They’re doing great things.
“I’m excited by the pace of change. Lifting the ban on onshore wind within 36 hours. GB Energy. It’s all good stuff – way too early to be disappointed.”
Sir Keir Starmer has unveiled the latest furry resident of Downing Street – Prince the Siberian kitten:
My colleague Genevieve Holl-Allen has more on the newest arrival to No 10
Sir Keir Starmer has a month to prove that his Government is not “fundamentally” dysfunctional, a senior Whitehall figure has said.
In a warning shot to the Prime Minister, the source said Sue Gray was “not of the party” and that only he could get a grip on the worsening situation.
The remarks come amid a bitter briefing war between top figures in Downing Street, and a public row over donations to Cabinet ministers.
On Saturday night, a No 10 source dismissed suggestions of a split and insisted the Government was “laser-focused” on delivering on voters’ priorities.
A poll on Saturday showed that Sir Keir’s approval rating had plummeted to its lowest level, and he was now more unpopular than Rishi Sunak.
Nick Gutteridge has the full story
Private schools should continue outreach work and providing bursaries once VAT on fees is introduced, the Education Secretary said.
Independent education will be hit with 20 per cent of VAT on fees from January, prompting reports that some schools may find themselves unable to continue taking part in community work and offering scholarships.
Asked about the reports, Bridget Phillipson told Times Radio: “I don’t accept that. Some of them have got very large incomes and actually a relatively small percentage of that income going towards bursaries.
“That list in the Sunday Times had some very wealthy schools with significant assets and big levels of income who aren’t putting a huge amount of that money towards bursaries and support in terms of partnership working with the state sector.
“Changes around VAT should not and must not impact on the work that they are doing around bursaries. There is an expectation of course that that would continue.”
David Lammy has condemned the “axis of renegades” helping Russia fight Ukraine, writes Jacob Freedland.
The Foreign Secretary told a panel on Ukraine at Labour Conference in Liverpool: “It’s important to take on this other threat that can also get lost in the noise.
“It’s the axis of renegades which sees Russia teaming up with Iran - we saw with the recent shipment of ballistic missiles - and teaming up with North Korea as well, and also the west is doing a lot to urge China not to throw its lot in, although we are concerned about equipment that’s making its way into Russia.
“We are doing all we can not just to squeeze Russia, but to squeeze those that would ensure that the weapons and means [to fight Ukraine] are used.”
Angela Rayner, the Deputy Prime Minister and Labour’s deputy leader, will address the main conference hall at 11.25am.
Pat McFadden, the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, and Darren Jones, the Chief Secretary to the Treasury, will also speak, as well as Lucy Powell, the Leader of the Commons.
An international speaker will address the conference at 2.15pm, before David Lammy, the Foreign Secretary, takes to the stage at 2.30pm.
Bridget Phillipson insisted Labour will eventually offer “some hope and optimism” as she defended cutting the winter fuel allowance for 10 million pensioners.
The Education Secretary was asked by Sky’s Sunday Morning with Trevor Phillips about the policy, which has led to warnings that hundreds of thousands of retirees could be plunged into fuel poverty.
“I take absolutely no relish in the fact that we’ve had to make this decision,” Ms Phillipson said.
“It was not a decision that we expected to make... Look, there was that huge gap in the public finances, £22 billion. The Tories knew that. They called an election, they walked away, and they left it to somebody else to sort out.
“We will fix it, by the way. We will sort this. We will get our economy back on a much firmer footing and we will deliver some hope and optimism about the difference that we can make.”
Both Sir Ed Davey, the Liberal Democrat leader, and Nigel Farage, the Reform leader, used their party conference speeches last week to accuse Sir Keir Starmer of “doom and gloom”.
Angela Rayner said she is “angry” about some of the coverage of Sue Gray, Sir Keir Starmer’s Chief of Staff.
“Sue Gray has been doing an incredible job and she’s got a huge amount of respect amongst the Cabinet,” she said.
“It angers me, as someone who has been a trade union rep in the past and who wants to bring workers’ rights, that somehow it’s OK to demonise workers in their workplace through the press and the media.
“I think Sue Gray has done an exceptional job and we are all working together to achieve for the British people.”
Ms Rayner also told the BBC: “I don’t accept that Sue Gray is part of a problem at all and I don’t accept the caricature of how Number 10 is working.”
Sue Gray will still be in a job by Christmas, Angela Rayner has said.
Sir Keir Starmer’s Chief of Staff has been the subject of negative briefings in recent weeks, while it emerged last week she is earning £3,000 more than the Prime Minister.
Some reports have suggested Ms Gray, who will stay away from Labour’s party conference in Liverpool, is set to leave her post shortly after the annual gathering.
But asked whether Ms Gray would still be in post at the end of the year, Ms Rayner, Sir Keir’s deputy, replied: “I think so, absolutely.”
Bridget Phillipson has admitted receiving £14,000 from Labour donor Lord Alli that helped pay for events to mark her 40th birthday.
The Education Secretary declared two donations from Lord Alli, who is also Sir Keir Starmer’s biggest personal donor, saying they were to “host a number of events”.
Speaking on Sky News, she admitted some of the cash was used to pay for a celebratory 40th birthday event held in December at the Hoare Memorial Hall, a venue which boasts “stunning views” of Westminster Abbey.
It came as a row over clothing donations accepted by senior party figures including Sir Keir and Angela Rayner, his deputy, threatened to overshadow the start of Labour’s conference in Liverpool.
Gaza protesters have already begun demonstrating at the gates of Labour conference this morning as day one gets underway in Liverpool, writes Genevieve Holl-Allen.
A van with the message “suspend all arms to Israel” emblazoned along both sides was being driven along the riverfront at 9:30am this morning.
Groups of demonstrators holding Palestine flags and placards with messages such as “Party of Crooks” and “Stop F-35s” were at the gates of the conference zone.
Sir Keir Starmer needs to reverse his “cruel” cuts to winter fuel payments, the head of Britain’s biggest trade union has warned.
Around 10 million retirees have been stripped of their winter fuel allowance this year, with the previously universal benefit now only going to those already in receipt of pension credit.
Sharon Graham, the general secretary of Unite the Union, told Sunday Morning with Trevor Phillips: “I think the priority that I’d like to hear from him is that he’s going to reverse the decision on the winter fuel allowance. It’s a cruel policy.
“He needs to reverse it. And I’d like him to say that he’s made a misstep and to reverse that policy. I’d also like him to say that we’re not going to take this country down austerity mark two.
“People voted for change. They need to see change. And he needs to reverse the winter fuel allowance [decision] and let people have that £300 they can put their heating on this winter.”
MPs accepting donations and gifts has been part and parcel of political life “for some time”, Angela Rayner has said.
The Deputy Prime Minister told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg; “MPs have accepted donations and gifts for years, all MPs do it. And what we’ve talked about is making sure we’re open and transparent about that.
“And that’s why the Prime Minister corrected the record when he was told he needed to do that.
“We want to make sure the Government are transparent. But gifts and donations have been a factor in our political life for some time… What Keir was saying in particular around some of the donations, including football and security, is that they shouldn’t land on taxpayers.”
Angela Rayner insisted she did not break any rules over her use of a donated New York apartment by millionaire Labour backer Lord Alli.
The Deputy Prime Minister told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: “First of all I didn’t go to New York with another person. That person went to New York and I met up with them and I met up with a number of friends while I was in New York.
“It was a personal holiday and I think I followed the rules. In fact I went above that and I wanted to do that to be transparent about the connection I had in the use of that apartment.”
Ms Rayner added: “I don’t believe I broke any rules. I had the use of the apartment and I disclosed that I had the use of that apartment.
“If anything I was overly transparent because I thought it was important that despite it being a personal holiday, because that person as a friend had already donated to me in the past for my deputy leadership…”
Good morning from day one of the annual Labour Party conference here in Liverpool.
What was supposed to be a victory lap for Sir Keir Starmer’s party after its general election triumph has been overshadowed by rows over gifts, donations and Sue Gray’s pay.
I will be guiding you through all of today’s developments.
author: Dominic Penna
Ben Riley-Smith
Jacob Freedland

Thank you for following today’s politics liveblog.
We will be back next week to bring you all the latest from the Conservative Party Conference in Birmingham.
Labour’s new climate envoy has previously expressed support for Extinction Rebellion, Amy Gibbons reports.
Rachel Kyte donned a badge bearing the environmental protest group’s logo in 2018 and warned people to “act now or get out of the way” as it prepared to launch a week of global action the following year.
She also praised Farhana Yamin, an activist who glued herself to the forecourt of the Shell’s headquarters in London as part of an Extinction Rebellion (XR) protest in 2019.
Ms Kyte, who has been appointed as the UK’s special representative for climate, does not hold an “official role” with Extinction Rebellion.
Read more on this story from The Telegraph’s Political Correspondent here
Sir Keir Starmer’s team should visit Germany to study Olaf Scholz’s election-winning strategy, Jonathan Ashworth has said.
The head of the influential Labour Together think tank, and ex-shadow Cabinet minister, said that it was “absolutely vital” that the party “learn the lessons” of others when seeking re-election.
Mr Ashworth told The House magazine: “Across the world, incumbents face challenges. Given that we are a new government and an incumbent government, when we’ll be seeking re-election it’s absolutely vital we learn the lessons.”
The public do not want the “sugary razzmatazz of Boris Johnson” and will respect someone who is “straight with them”, Jonathan Ashworth has said.
The former shadow Cabinet minister, who is now the head of the influential Labour Together think tank, defended the tone of Sir Keir Starmer in recent weeks, which has been criticised as being too “gloomy”.
He told The House magazine: “The British public will respect someone if he levels with them and is straight with them, rather than the sugary razzmatazz of Boris Johnson and others in recent times… But I know exactly what you mean. Kamala Harris is talking about joy, I’m sure there’ll be joy here as well.”
He said: “It’s not all doom and gloom… I don’t think it feels doom and gloomy. Just honest.”
Having been in the United States over the Democratic convention, Ashworth adds: “The British public will respect someone if he levels with them and is straight with them, rather than the sugary razzmatazz of Boris Johnson and others in recent times… But I know exactly what you mean. Kamala Harris is talking about joy, I’m sure there’ll be joy here as well.”
The Tories presided over a decade of “acquiescence, tolerance and promotion of racism”, Baroness Warsi has said.
The peer quit the Conservative Party last night after the party launched an investigation into “divisive” comments.
She faced criticism earlier this month when she celebrated the acquittal of a protester who was found not guilty despite carrying a placard accusing Rishi Sunak and Suella Braverman of being “coconuts”.
Writing on X, Baroness Warsi said: “Thank you to colleagues from across Parliament who have reached out with kind messages and solidarity.
Thank you also to the likes of James (Cleverly) and others who are providing me with an opportunity to revisit the last ten years of inaction, acquiescence, tolerance and promotion of racism that poisoned the public discourse leading to violence on our streets.
“Damaged our country and destroyed our party. I kept the receipts and look forward to publishing them,” she added.
Kemi Badenoch will face off against Tom Tugendhat and Robert Jenrick will go up against James Cleverly as they compete for members’ support at the Conservative Party Conference.
Ms Badenoch, seen as being on the Right of the party, will face questions from party members on Sunday alongside the former security minister, considered a more moderate candidate.
A similar match up will take place later on on Sunday between Mr Jenrick and the shadow home secretary.
The Conservative Party Conference in Birmingham, which kicks off this weekend, will feature the four leadership candidates as top billing as they take part in the so-called “beauty parade” in front of members.
The four hopefuls will take to the main stage on Monday morning one after another to give speeches to the party faithful about their vision for the future of the party.
Other than the leadership candidates, the most senior Tory figure to appear on the main stage will be Jeremy Hunt, the shadow Chancellor. As was widely rumoured, Rishi Sunak will not appear on the main stage.
Fewer Labour Party members spent time on the campaign trail this year than in any of the last three general elections, it has emerged.
More than four in ten (43pc) of Labour members said they spent no time campaigning for Sir Keir Starmer in the general election campaign this year, up from 40 per cent in 2019.
More members reported being active campaigners during the 2017 and 2015 campaigns, despite Labour not ultimately winning any of the contests, according to the Queen Mary University and Sussex University party members project.
The Government has been warned cash injection for local councils billed by ministers as a mitigation to the winter fuel raid will not be enough to protect vulnerable pensioners, Amy Gibbons reports.
Emma Reynolds, the pensions minister, said the extension of the Household Support Fund would help protect those “just above the threshold” for means-tested benefits.
But The Telegraph understands that the guidance sent to councils in charge of administering the grant does not contain a single mention of the winter fuel cut, prompting fears the money will be swallowed up by competing demands.
Teresa O’Neill, a Tory peer and London’s longest serving council leader, said the fund can’t be easily targeted and “will not make up for the money vulnerable and low-income pensioners are losing”.
Dame Priti Patel, the former home secretary, has also raised the issue in a letter to the Work and Pensions Secretary.
Hitting Sir Keir with one of his own classic attack lines, she told The Telegraph it was a “sticking plaster” for a cut that will “hurt the very people society should be protecting”.
A spokesman for the Department for Work and Pensions said: “Local Authorities will continue to be able to distribute this lifeline funding to all those in need in their local area
Rachel Reeves should cut public sector workers’ “extremely valuable” pensions at her maiden Budget, a leading think tank has said, Eir Nolsoe reports.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) told the Chancellor that there is a “good case” for lowering pensions for public sector workers to fund future pay rises after the Government granted inflation-busting settlements to doctors, teachers and nurses.
The report published ahead of the Budget on Oct 30 warns that to overcome recruitment difficulties the Treasury must reform rather than just raise pay amid a surging wage bill.
It also noted the disparity between public sector and private sector pensions: “Public sector pensions remain extremely valuable relative to private sector comparators. The pension contributions from public sector employers are higher than those often seen for even high-earning private sector employees.”
Read more on this story here
Defence Secretary John Healey is looking at a rumoured Israeli ground invasion into Lebanon “really carefully”, he has said.
Mr Healey said on Friday airstrikes and rocket fire exchanged between Israel and Hezbollah present a “risk that this escalates into something that is much wider and much more serious”.
Speaking to broadcasters, Mr Healey said his “first concern remains the safety of British nationals in Lebanon”.
He added: “The travel advice remains the same – don’t go to Lebanon. If you are in Lebanon, then get out and there are still commercial flights leaving so people can do that.
“But I left Labour conference earlier this week to chair a Cobra committee in Government because we are making the preparations you’d expect of Government ahead of any potential developments in the future.”
Asked about the rumoured ground invasion, Mr Healey replied: “We’re watching this really carefully. That will be a matter for the Israelis.
Kemi Badenoch has hit back at critics who condemned her for saying that she “became working class” after getting a job at McDonald’s as a teenager.
The Tory party candidate worked at the fast food chain aged 16 when she moved to the UK to study.
She told GB News last week: “I grew up in a middle class family, but I became working class when I was 16 working at McDonald’s.”
The former business secretary suffered a backlash over the comments, including from Labour minister Chris Bryant who said: “I’m not sure that’s how it works.”
Responding to the criticism, Ms Badenoch told The Spectator: “I made a passing comment about being working class and I’m amazed at the number of people who have written articles off the back of it, ‘Oh is she working class?’”
“I think there are lots of humanities graduates who may not know how to solve climate change, net zero productivity. But if it’s time to ask whether somebody is working class or not, they get their pens out like, ‘this is what we know how to do.’”
Donald Trump shared a two-hour dinner with Sir Keir Starmer after heaping praise on the “popular” Prime Minister, Nick Gutteridge reports.
The former president said that Sir Keir had run a “great” election campaign before they met for the first time at Trump Tower in New York.
The Prime Minister asked for the meeting as he looks to build ties with the Republican candidate ahead of the US election in November.
Read the full story from The Telegraph’s Chief Political Correspondent on what happened in New York here
Sir Keir Starmer is as unpopular as Rishi Sunak was when he called the general election, a new poll has found.
The Prime Minister has a net approval rating of -27, according to polling by More in Common, a score which has fallen by 38 points since July.
Rishi Sunak had a net approval rating of -28 when he called the general election in early May.
Luke Tryl, the director of the think tank, said: “After some tough headlines this week the Starmer slide in approval has continued.”
Pension credit claims have hit almost 75,000 in the last two months amid Government efforts to boost take-up after the axing of universal winter fuel payments.
Department for Work and Pensions figures released this morning showed the Government received around 74,400 pension credit claims in the eight weeks since July 29, when Rachel Reeves announced that the winter fuel allowance would be means-tested.
This is up from 29,500 claims in the eight weeks before the announcement.
Nigel Farage has said Rachel Reeves should cut UK funding of the “scaremongering” World Health Organisation (WHO) and spend the money on winter fuel payments for pensioners, Gordon Rayner reports.
Britain sends around £200 million per year to the WHO, a figure that is likely to leap into the billions thanks to a pandemic preparedness treaty currently under negotiation.
The Reform UK leader says the WHO was “empire building” by proposing a global monitoring system for potential pandemics the cost of which will dwarf the organisation’s current budget.
Read more from The Telegraph’s Associate Editor here
Russell Findlay has said that he is “not the same” as other politicians and that he understands the “frustrations” of voters as he is elected as the leader of the Scottish Tory party.
In his acceptance speech, he said: “I want to deliver a message to people across Scotland who don’t feel that anyone represents them, who are scarred by the divisiveness and the fringe obsessions of the Scottish Parliament, who feel let down by politicians of every single party, sometimes including ours. Who think that politicians are all the same.
“If you feel that way, I get it. But I’m not the same. I’m not a career politician. I understand your frustrations.”
He added: “Everyone must come together as one united team. Let’s start the hard work right now to win back public trust.”
The newly-elected leader of the Scottish Conservatives has made a jibe at Sir Keir Starmer over his conference speech gaffe where he mistakenly said “sausages” rather than “hostages”.
Russell Findlay, the new Scottish Tory leader, said in his speech: “I want to start by thanking everyone who put their faith in me and to thank obviously every single member who voted for me and every sausage, uh, sorry, sorry, every supporter who worked so hard for my campaign.”
Sir Keir made the memorable slip-up on Tuesday, whilst he was delivering his first Labour conference speech as Prime Minister.
In a key part of the address about a ceasefire in Gaza, he called for the “return of the sausages” before correcting himself and saying hostages.
Russell Findlay has become the new leader of the Scottish Conservatives, it has been announced.
The party’s justice spokesman secured an overwhelming victory in the leadership election to succeed Douglas Ross.
Mr Findlay won 2,565 votes, with his nearest rival Murdo Fraser securing 1,189 and Meghan Gallacher 403 votes.
He will be heading to Birmingham within 24 hours of taking his role for the Conservative Party Conference.
Rachel Reeves is considering abandoning her pledge to abolish non-dom status over fears it may fail to raise any money.
Labour included a pledge to end the tax perk for wealthy residents who are domiciled overseas in its manifesto, hoping the policy would raise £1 billion a year.
However, Treasury officials are concerned that the move will force so many wealthy foreigners to leave that the measure will backfire.
Government officials said they would consider changing the details of the policy to make it less punishing to non-doms, with reducing the amount of inheritance tax they would have to pay thought to be one of the options under consideration.
Read more on this story here
Wes Streeting has said he will reduce the NHS’ “overreliance” on migrants to staff the health service.
In an interview on GB News’ Chopper’s Political Political Podcast, the Health Secretary said that the UK tended to “nick people from elsewere” to work as nurses in the NHS rather than training homegrown talent.
Mr Streeting said: “I think it’s part of my responsibility as the Health and Social Care Secretary to help the Home Secretary reduce net migration in this country, because we do have an overreliance.
“And two things can be true at the same time. Firstly, we’re really lucky that we’ve got some amazing people from around the world who come to our country to provide great care in our NHS and social care system, and I’m grateful to those people, but we’re also overreliant.
He added: “And I think, frankly, for a long time now, we’ve had a culture that says we won’t bother to train our own homegrown talent.
“We’ll just nick people from elsewhere, which is, um, I think unfair on those countries, but also unfair on people in our own country who might love the chance to work.”
New York’s Times Square is a “glimpse of the future” for London’s Oxford Street, Sadiq Khan has said.
The London Mayor earlier this month announced plans to pedestrianise one of London’s busiest shopping streets, and has been backed by Angela Rayner.
In a video filmed in New York, Mr Khan met with city officials to discuss how Times Square was redeveloped, which he said was a “glimpse of the future for Oxford Street”.
Tom Tugendhat has said that prolific offenders should be forced to serve their entire sentence in jail, Charles Hymas reports.
The Conservative Party leadership contender and former security minister said repeat criminals should be excluded from the current automatic release rules under which offenders can be freed 40 per cent or 50 per cent of the way through their sentence.
Under these rules, offenders are freed for the remaining 50 per cent or 60 per cent of their sentence under licence, which can place conditions including where they live, who they contact and where they can travel. Any breach means they can be recalled to prison to serve the remainder of their sentence.
Speaking ahead of the Tory conference in Birmingham, Mr Tugendhat, one of four remaining leadership contenders, said they should serve their full sentence in jail and then spend the rest of their lives on licence, subjecting them to a lifetime of supervision by probation where any breach could see them returned to jail.
Read more on this story here
Sir Keir Starmer once said that an endorsement from Donald Trump showed that Boris Johnson “isn’t fit to be Prime Minister”, it has emerged.
The Prime Minister said in 2019 that the backing of Mr Trump “tells you everything you need to know about what is wrong with Boris Johnson’s politics”.
The tweet resurfaced after the US presidential candidate praised Sir Keir last night in New York as being “very nice” before the pair met for dinner.
The Prime Minister shared a BBC article in June 2019 that reported that the then-US president said Mr Johson would be an “excellent” choice for Tory leader during the party’s leadership race.
Sir Keir wrote on X before he became Labour leader: “An endorsement from Donald Trump tells you everything you need to know about what is wrong with Boris Johnson’s politics and why he isn’t fit to be Prime Minister.”
James Cleverly has criticised Baroness Warsi over her celebration of the acquittal of a protestor who carried a placard accusing Rishi Sunak and Suella Braverman of being “coconuts”.
The Tory leadership contender said that the slur which indicates that a black person is acting on behalf of white people was “unacceptable”.
It comes after the peer quit the Tories after the party launched an investigation into “divisive” comments.
Mr Cleverly said: “‘You’re not properly black if you’re a Tory’ is a particularly pernicious attack.
“I’ve been called a coconut too many times to laugh it off. It hasn’t held me back or brought me down, but a Conservative peer not recognising the abuse of other black colleagues is unacceptable.”
Boris Johnson tried to persuade Prince Harry not to leave the UK with his wife Meghan, the former prime minister has revealed.
Mr Johnson said he was asked to give the Duke of Sussex a “manly pep talk” to convince him not to step back from his royal duties.
Officials from Buckingham Palace and Downing Street are said to have believed the last-minute intervention in January 2020 could have succeeded in talking Harry out of his decision.
Read more on this story here
Robert Jenrick has criticised the BBC for describing Hezbollah a “Lebanese armed group”, rather than as a terrorist organisation, in its news coverage.
The Conservative leadership candidate pointed to the status of Hezbollah’s military wing as a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.
The former Home Office minister claimed the broadcaster had “learned nothing” from the criticism over its descriptions of Hamas after the October 7 attacks.
Sharing a BBC article on X, he wrote: “Have the BBC learnt nothing?
“First Hamas, now ‘the Lebanese armed group, Hezbollah’.
“Our national broadcaster should call proscribed terrorist organisations, what they are.”
Sir Keir Starmer has laughed off the Labour conference speech slip-up which saw him accidentally refer to Israeli hostages as “sausages”, Nick Gutteridge writes in New York.
The Prime Minister admitted he had “mangled” the key part of the address and said the error had given journalists the “opportunity to rib me”.
His remarks, during a trip to New York, are the first time he has commented on the gaffe that sparked a slew of articles and jokes on social media.
Read more from The Telegraph’s Chief Political Correspondent here
US president hopeful Donald Trump “needs to be called out” if he starts “caging Mexican children”, should he win the presidential election, Emily Thornberry has said.
Asked about remarks Ms Thornberry made in 2019, when she alleged Mr Trump had “grabbed women and boasted about it” and “tried to close borders with Muslim-majority countries”, the foreign affairs committee chairwoman replied: “If he’s president and he starts caging Mexican children, then that needs to be called out.”
She told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We are actually in a really strong position now, in that if you think about all the other G7 countries, we are a country that we have just had an election, we have a progressive Government with a large majority and stability in front of us – a good five years of the same leader.
“And if you look at the other G7 countries, they don’t necessarily have that.”
Asked Mr Trump should be labelled a “racist”, the former shadow Cabinet minister said: “It depends how he is behaving.
“I mean, he seems – he styles it out somewhat, doesn’t he, these allegations? I mean, you know, we hear about the dogs and cats and so on just a few weeks ago.”
In a reference to Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer’s meeting with Mr Trump, she added: “If I was at dinner with someone who said things like that, then I would call it out. But I don’t imagine that the conversation moved on to things like that at that dinner.”
A deal on a youth mobility scheme between the UK and the European Union could be reached, ministers believe.
A formal proposal for a scheme, like a “gap year” for EU citizens, is expected to be approve by the bloc which will then be presented to the UK Government in weeks, The Times reported.
Pedro Serrano, the EU ambassador to the UK, told Times Radio: “This is about ensuring that our youth continues to get together to know each other. And if we have a mechanism that allows young British citizens to go for a gap year, for example, to any of 27 states within the European Union — to do a bit of learning and get pay … while they’re there, why not?”
A Government source told the newspaper that ministers believed there was a “landing zone” for an agreement which would see greater reciprocal access for young people.
The Government “shouldn’t pull our punches” if it disagrees with Donald Trump, Emily Thornberry has said.
The foreign affairs select committee chairwoman said that it was “important” to “build a relationship” with the US presidential candidate, after Sir Keir Starmer had dinner with him last night.
But she told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme: “I do think that if there are things the American president does or says that we disagree with, then we shouldn’t pull our punches.”
The former shadow Cabinet minister said: “Donald Trump may be the president of the United States in a couple of months’ time so of course, it’s important to have meetings with him and to build a relationship with him.
“Whatever criticisms one may have of Donald Trump, the point is that the office of president is one that needs to be properly respected and the Americans are very close friends of ours.”
She added: “I think that this is an initial meeting, so there needs to be a certain amount of relationship building and we take it from there.
Good morning and welcome to today’s politics liveblog.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/09.title: Fresh attack on Van Gogh’s Sunflowers after Just Stop Oil activists jailed
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/09.subtitle: Protesters target same painting that Phoebe Plummer and Anna Holland threw soup at in 2022
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/09.text:
Just Stop Oil has thrown soup over two of Vincent Van Gogh’s Sunflowers paintings in “a sign of defiance” after two of their members were jailed for a similar protest.
On Friday, three protesters entered the Van Gogh “Poets and Lovers” exhibition at the National Gallery in London and threw soup over Sunflowers 1889 and Sunflowers 1888.
It comes after Phoebe Plummer and Anna Holland were jailed on Friday for two years and 20 months respectively for throwing soup over the same 1888 painting in October 2022.
Just Stop Oil claims similar actions of solidarity took place in Berlin, where protesters gathered outside the British embassy holding “Solidarity with the Soup Throwers” signs.
The National Gallery said the three activists had been arrested and the paintings remain unharmed after the incident at 2.30pm.
A statement said: “The paintings were removed from display and examined by a conservator and are unharmed. We are aiming to reopen the exhibition as soon as possible.”
In a video on social media, one protester said: “Future generations will regard these prisoners of conscience to be on the right side of history.”
Holland and Plummer, both 22, were found guilty of criminal damage at Southwark Crown Court in July.
During their trial, it was heard the activists, who denied damaging the painting, caused as much as £10,000 worth of damage to the frame, which prosecutors said was “a piece of art in itself”.
The protesters, wearing Just Stop Oil T-shirts, threw two tins of Heinz tomato soup over the 1888 work in October 2022, before kneeling down in front of the painting and gluing their hands to the wall beneath it.
Visitors were escorted out by security staff, who then shut the doors to the room containing the painting.
Raj Chada, defending Holland, said the women “did check” that the painting was protected by a glass cover before throwing the soup.
Plummer, representing herself, told the hearing: “My choice today is to accept whatever sentence I receive with a smile.
“It is not just myself being sentenced today, or my co-defendants, but the foundations of democracy itself.”
Painted in Arles in the south of France in August 1888, Van Gogh’s painting shows 15 sunflowers standing in a yellow pot against a yellow background.
The priceless work was the second from the National Gallery to be selected as a target for protest action by Just Stop Oil in 2022, with two supporters gluing themselves to John Constable’s The Hay Wain in July of that year.
In a video from the attack, Plummer was heard saying: “What is worth more, art or life? Is it worth more than food? Worth more than justice?
“Are you more concerned about the protection of a painting, or the protection of our planet and people? The cost of living crisis is part of the cost of oil crisis.”
Sentencing the eco-activists, Judge Christopher Hehir said the painting could have been “seriously damaged or even destroyed”.
“Soup might have seeped through the glass,” he continued. “You couldn’t have cared less if the painting was damaged or not. You had no right to do what you did to Sunflowers.”
Judge Hehir interrupted Plummer when she referred to herself as a “political prisoner”. He said: “This is not helping your case, you’re reading from a Just Stop Oil script, and I’ve heard it all before.
“You understand we don’t have political prisoners in this country, there are people suffering in dungeons all over the world. What you’re doing is making an offensive comparison.”
He said the pair had “crossed the line from concerned campaigner to fanatic”.
Addressing Plummer directly, he added: “The suggestion that you and others like you who are convicted by juries of your peers are somehow a political prisoner is ludicrous, self-indulgent and offensive.
“Perhaps some day you will come to realise that but I fear that day is a long way off.”
Plummer also received a three-month jail term for her part in a slow march that caused long tailbacks in west London in November 2023.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/09.title: Why are our water companies so crap?
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/09.subtitle: Despite Britain’s reputation for rainfall, we are preparing to import water from Norway – a deal that highlights this country’s incompetence
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/09.text:
It’s pouring with rain outside. The roof lights above my head are getting a hammering, the stream is turning into a dark and muddy river and water is pooling in the yard. A friend in Warwickshire has sent me a photo of the road outside his front door, currently a raging torrent, and a newsflash has popped up on my phone to show a platform at Birmingham New Street under water.
After what felt like two and a half days of dry summer, normal service resumes. Britain is under a deluge; football stadiums are flooded; and there are, as I write, 67 flood warnings currently flashing on the dashboard of the Environment Agency.
So maybe it’s apt – this is modern Britain after all – that on Friday, news leaks (lol) of a deal between Southern Water and Norway to ship drinking water to south-east England.
Thus, when the next drought occurs – which at the moment, I grant you, feels unlikely – their 4.7 million customers can rely on a daily pour of 45 million litres courtesy of the glacial waters of the Geirangerfjord, the Aurlandsfjord, the Naeroyfjord, and the Lysefjord.
And I suggest you attempt to say those words because it will render you exactly as you should be with this news: that is, speechless.
As the saying goes, “water, water everywhere nor any drop to drink.” Nor bathe in, nor water the plants with, nor add to your beer casks, nor hose into your paddling pool. For such is our incompetence that we now compete internationally for the title of ‘Most Stupidly Administered Country in the World’.
And just as Sir Keir Starmer parades his newly elected self on the international stage and tells the world, as he informed us followers on Instagram this morning: “We are returning the UK to responsible global leadership”, our actual bosses – I’m thinking NHS administrators, rail and road infrastructure leaders – tell the real story.
In the words of Southern Water’s managing director for water, Tim McMahon: “We’ve adapted our plans to deliver an environmentally resilient solution that meets the requirements of the Environment Agency’s abstraction licence reductions.” Which sends me scrabbling to the glossary.
Maybe you agree that the EA’s abstraction licence reductions are vital. (In layman’s terms, they are part of a plan to protect Britain’s fish, rivers and other wildlife habitats by limiting the amount of water firms are allowed to abstract.) Or you think that the weather is a red herring, since it will take years before our creaking water infrastructure has been overhauled and we have a better way of storing rainwater.
But that’s not what Greenpeace is saying. Their chief scientist, Doug Parr, lays the blame squarely at the door of Southern Water, which, he says, has neglected its own infrastructure “for decades”.
And he’s not happy with the plan for water to be shipped over in giant Tetra-Pak style cartons, as this would cause “permanent damage to local ecosystems” in Norway. Indeed, the tourists on their cruise ships, not to mention the auks, puffins and sheathbills, might be wondering where the hell their water has gone.
So why can’t we store it here when it rains? As it seems to do. All the time. There are examples of some good practice with, for example, Wessex Water, managing supplies in my patch of West Somerset, bucking the trend with considerable competence, and even employing (locally based) humans who answer their telephones.
A friend of mine once bought a property on the Western Cape of South Africa. It was the former home of a leading politician and one day he discovered a secret: a very long pipe that brought water from nearby Cape Town that had been used to irrigate his thirsty vines.
If a corrupt politician can find water for his wine in Africa, surely a British utility company can contain, manage or at least blag some of the wet stuff from its drenched neighbours rather than raping the fjords of Norway.
